NISA · deglacial meltwater · HadCM3 impulse responses

Meltwater Discharge Explorer

Meltwater from nine ice-sheet drainage regions, carried by the ocean. The globe shows how the surface δ¹⁸O anomaly spreads, decade by decade. The chart shows what reaches one proxy site and where it came from. Pick a reconstruction and an AMOC pathway, then play or drag through the deglaciation.

How the model works

The forward model has five steps. A reconstruction gives the meltwater per drainage region. The ocean model says how a short pulse from each region spreads. Adding up those pulses, decade by decade and in the AMOC mode of the time, gives the surface anomaly everywhere, which is then read at the core or cave.

The whole chain

Asite(t) = Σr Σx wsite(x) · Σk Fr(t − k) · hr, m(t−k)(x, k)
Fr
source-region δ¹⁸O anomaly of region r (step 1)
hr,m
surface response to a 10-yr pulse, AMOC mode m (step 2)
m(t − k)
mode at the time the water was released (step 4)
wsite
±2° box for cores, moisture uptake for land sites (step 5)
Σk, Σr
over the 50 decades of the response, and over the 9 regions
Asite
δ¹⁸O anomaly at the site, to compare with the proxy record
Assumptions: the response is linear in discharge (no saturation), the kernels come from 17.8 ka boundary conditions, and only the surface layer is used. Pulse runs: xpran (cold), xprao (zonal) and xpujc (merid), each after 10 years of its constant-input parent (xpraj, xprak, xpram). The merid parent is not the paper's merid run, xpral.
Forcing panel: GLAC-1D regional discharge, 24–8 ka, with regions in the explorer's colours. The pulse-response and pathway curves are schematic shapes, not model output.
